**Title:** In-vivo CRISPR/Base-Editing "One-Shot" Therapies Targeting PCSK9.

**Authors:** Benjamin Nelson, Amit Khera

**Journal:** Current atherosclerosis reports
**Publication Date:** 2026-10-15
**DOI:** 10.1007/s11883-026-01470-8

**Full Text Available:** Yes
**Full Text URL:** https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC13672524/


**Abstract:**
To assess and present the current state of gene editing for reduction of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) with emphasis on technology and ongoing trials for genetic editing of protein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9).

To assess and present the current state of gene editing for reduction of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) with emphasis on technology and ongoing trials for genetic editing of protein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9).

There are two ongoing clinical trials in humans to edit PCSK9 using CRISPR-Cas9 base editing technology packaged within lipid nanoparticles (LNPs). Preliminary interim and preclinical data suggest that this strategy is effective for long-term reduction of PCSK9 and LDL-C following a single IV infusion.

Monoclonal antibodies that neutralize circulating PCSK9 have demonstrated the utility of PCSK9 inhibition for reducing LDL-C and ASCVD. Although there is an increasing number of pharmacologic strategies for inhibiting PCSK9, gene editing is an attractive option due to its potential to permanently reduce circulating PCSK9 levels and by extension LDL-C and ASCVD. There are two ongoing clinical trials in humans investigating the safety and efficacy of gene editing for PCSK9 with encouraging preliminary results. In this review, we will describe the background of PCSK9 as a target, the gene editing machinery and the preliminary results. We also explore the unique safety challenges of this technology and propose considerations for appropriate patient populations to maintain net positive benefits despite unknowns.

Keywords: Protein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9), Low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C), Atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) risk, Gene editing, CRISPR-Cas9

Atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) is the leading cause of death in the developed world, and elevated low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) is a major risk factor for its development and progression. There are many therapies currently available that are proven to lower LDL-C and cardiovascular morbidity and mortality. These drugs target mechanisms involved in LDL-C synthesis, absorption or clearance and are available in a variety of pharmacologic modalities, including small molecules, monoclonal antibodies and interfering RNAs. These drugs have become important pillars in reducing ASCVD and have saved countless lives in recent decades; however, for some patients, available options fall short of optimal control of LDL-C. Gene editing strategies are now emerging as “one-shot” options for lifelong reduction of LDL-C with clinical trials currently underway. In this review, we will discuss ongoing efforts to harness CRISPR-Cas9 genomic engineering technology to reduce LDL-C and ASCVD by genetic ablation of proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9).

Proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9) is a protein that is synthesized in many tissues whence it is secreted into serum, with the liver being the dominant source of circulating PCSK9 protein. Its importance in lipid biology emerged from studying human populations with very low LDL levels, where PCSK9-inactivating genetic variants were found to confer a dose-dependent reduction in LDL-C and by extension ASCVD risk [1, 2]. Circulating serum PCSK9 reduces hepatocyte LDL receptor (LDLR) expression by increasing turnover and decreasing the functional half-life of the receptor [3]. Thus, lower circulating PCSK9 results in increased LDL receptor density and greater LDL particle clearance (Fig. 1).

Regulation of LDLR expression on hepatocyte surface by PCSK9. Binding of LDL particles to the LDLR on hepatocytes induces endocytosis and catabolism of the LDL particle. In the absence of PCSK9, LDLR are sorted away from the LDL particle and are directed back to the Golgi apparatus for re-expression on the cell surface. In the presence of PCSK9, LDLR is not recycled back to the surface, which reduces the number of LDLR under steady state conditions

Accordingly, PCSK9 has become a major pharmaceutical target for LDL-C-lowering, with neutralizing monoclonal antibodies being the most popular modality (Table 1). Currently there are two commercially-available, FDA-approved antibodies, alirocumab and evolocumab. These drugs have been shown to decrease serum LDL by 60–70%, even on background therapy with a statin, and reduce ASCVD risk in secondary prevention patients as well as those without prior clinical ASCVD but at higher risk [4–6]. They are typically administered as a subcutaneous injection every other week and are very well tolerated. Although monoclonal antibodies have rapidly become a major pillar in lipid management, some patients develop allergies or are unable to auto-inject medications, even if infrequently.

Comparison of currently available PCSK9-targeting therapies

Fortunately, PCSK9 is also targetable by many other modalities. Longer-acting interfering RNA technology, named inclisiran, has also been developed to silence PCSK9 mRNA in the liver, with maintenance dosing by subcutaneous injection every 6 months. Inclisiran has proven quite capable in lowering LDL-C, around 40–50% even in heterozygous FH, though outcome trials are currently ongoing [7–9]. More recently lerodalcibep-liga was developed as a first-in-class antibody-mimetic, known as an adnectin, which is now commercially available as a once monthly injection [10]. Orally bioavailable inhibitors have also recently demonstrated efficacy, with first-in-class, FDA-approved macrocyclic peptide inhibitor, enlicitide decanoate, reducing LDL-C by 57.1% [11]. Oral small molecule PCSK9 inhibitors are also in ongoing efficacy trials [12, 13].

Recent evidence has emerged suggesting extrahepatic and intracellular roles for PCSK9 as well, pointing to potential roles in inflammation, viral immunity and intracellular stress responses [14–16]. It has been hypothesized that PCSK9 may have evolved its role in LDL regulation to prevent exploitation of the LDLR for cell entry by an ancient viral or bacterial threat, although no such infectious threat is known to currently exist. Therefore, when considering efficacy and adverse effects of the myriad emerging pharmacologic options for PCSK9 inhibition, it may be important to consider the compartment of PCSK9 targeted by each drug, i.e. circulating pool for monoclonals, liver intracellular and secreted pool for siRNAs. Orally bioavailable small molecules and peptides could potentially target whole-body PCSK9, including secreted and intracellular pools, however, they may only inhibit certain interactions of PCSK9, such as its interface with the LDL receptor, while potentially preserving others.

CRISPR-Cas9 technology selectively targets specific sequences within the genome, allowing for permanent elimination or modification of the DNA blueprint. It is derived from machinery that evolved to digest genomes of invading bacteriophages, serving as a form of adaptive immunity in prokaryotes [17]. In its simplest form, a CRISPR-Cas9 complex is composed of two parts: a hairpin (or duplex in older versions) RNA called a guide RNA (gRNA) that is complementary to the DNA sequence being targeted and an enzyme called Cas9 which allows genomic locus targeting and editing [18]. These two components make up the fully self-functioning Cas9 ribonucleoprotein (RNP).

A human somatic nucleus contains approximately 6 billion base pairs (bp) of DNA, among which the Cas9 RNP must localize specifically to only one or two 20-bp regions (two copies for targets in autosomes, one or two for sex chromosomes). Targeting is initiated through recognition of short DNA sequences known as protospacer adjacent motifs (PAMs), which interact directly with a Cas9 protein domain [19–21]. Once the PAM has weakly bound the RNP to the genome, Cas9 exposes genomic DNA to the sgRNA to create a highly stable RNA: DNA hybrid helix – this structure anchors the enzyme to the genome on one DNA strand and leaves the other complementary strand exposed for editing. Next, the DNA is cleaved on both strands by nuclease domains to generate a double-stranded DNA break (DSB), followed by dissociation of the complex from the genome. The lesion is then repaired by an endogenous DNA repair mechanism known as non-homologous end joining (NHEJ), which non-specifically joins broken DNA ends using an error-prone process that eventually leads to insertions and deletions of random sequences [22]. While this DSB-mediated strategy is elegant in its simplicity and very efficient in disrupting gene expression, the final sequence produced is inherently heterogenous due to the random nature of NHEJ.

Base editing is a popular alternative strategy to DSBs that seeks to increase the fidelity and reproducibility of the CRISPR-Cas9 system. In this strategy, a base editor changes the chemical structure (and the pairing complementarity) of nucleotides within the targeted sequence. Currently, adenine base editors (ABEs) are most common due their high efficiency and fidelity, though cytosine editors are also available and improving.

Similar to the DSB strategy described above, a sgRNA is used to home the RNP complex to the target sequence, however, the Cas9 enzyme has been recombinantly fused to an additional enzyme called a base editor, and one of the Cas9 DNA cleavage domains has been inactivated, which results in a single-stranded break (rather than DSB as occurs with wild-type enzyme) on the RNA-duplexed (non-edited) strand [23]. ABEs convert adenines on the free strand to inosine, which is read as guanine by DNA-reading enzymes during repair, replication or transcription. The nicked strand is then repaired by endogenous machinery using the edited strand as a template. Inosine may be further converted to guanine by endogenous repair machinery, though this is difficult to assess since sequencing techniques also read inosine as guanine. Replication of the DNA will produce a copy strand containing guanine in the edited position.

ABEs function most efficiently within a sweet spot called the editing window, the width of which varies depending on the particular ABE enzyme used. Within this window, ABE function is limited mostly by accessibility to the DNA substrate due to spatial constraints, and any adenine within this window may be edited with varying efficiency. Undesirable edits within the window are called bystander mutations. Therefore, although base editing does not produce random insertions, deletions and translocations as wildtype enzyme does, there is still some heterogeneity in the final sequence if there are multiple adenines in the target sequence since not all may be converted with the same efficiency. Ideally a therapeutic target should contain only one adenine within the editing window to ensure a homogenous edit.

Many therapeutic gene-elimination strategies target protein-coding regions or splice sites to cause premature protein termination and thus gene inactivation [24, 25]. Targeting the splice site donor or acceptor results in a retained intron, which usually results in a premature stop codon. Furthermore, when a ribosome encounters a stop codon sufficiently early in the transcript, it triggers an endogenous mRNA quality control pathway known as non-sense mediated decay, which degrades the mRNA transcript, resulting typically in negligible amounts of truncated protein.

Serum LDL-C levels are determined in large part by steady state dynamics balancing synthesis and clearance by the liver [26]. Accordingly, most current LDL-C lowering therapies target proteins residing or synthesized in the liver with the exceptions of ezetimibe which targets dietary cholesterol absorption via intestinal Niemann-Pick C1-like 1 (NPC1L1), bile acid sequestrants and apheresis. Conveniently, due to its professional role in clearing lipophilic particles from circulation, the liver is remarkably efficient in taking up chemically engineered lipid nanoparticles (LNPs), which may carry a variety of payloads including RNA molecules encoding gene editing machinery [27, 28]. In current use, these LNPs are administered in a single intravenous infusion.

The surface of the particle is coated in a mixture of PEGylated and cationic lipids. These LNPs are laden with gRNA that is complementary to a target genomic sequence as well as a messenger RNA (mRNA) that encodes the Cas9-ABE enzyme. Upon infusion, these particles become coated with serum proteins, most notably ApoE, which facilitate receptor-mediated endocytosis into the liver and release of the payload into the cytoplasm of the hepatocyte [29]. The mRNA is then engaged by ribosomes and translated into the Cas9-ABE apoenzyme. The nascent Cas9-ABE then binds the co-delivered sgRNA to make a fully functional holoenzyme which is imported into the nucleus by an endogenous mechanism. Inside the nucleus, Cas9-ABE scans chromatin for sequences complementary to the gRNA leading to therapeutic gene editing (Fig. 2).

Uptake of LNPs into the liver and expression of editing machinery. LNPs are introduced to the circulation by intravenous infusion. They are then bound by LDLR or ASGPR (in the case of GalNAc-modified LNPs) which facilitates endocytosis and release of the base editor mRNA and the gRNA targeting the PCSK9 gene. The mRNA is then translated into the base editor protein, which binds the gRNA to complete the ribonucleoprotein complex. The complex is then transported into the nucleus by endogenous machinery. The complex scans the genome to find the PCSK9 locus and then edits a specific adenine, converting it to inosine which is analogous to guanine. The resulting mutation disrupts the splicing of the PCSK9 pre-mRNA, resulting in a non-functional transcript, effectively eliminating expression of PCSK9 from the targeted cell

LNPs enter the liver via receptor-mediated endocytosis, which depends heavily upon LDL receptors. Because of role of the LDL receptor in LNP uptake, there has been concern that patients with homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia, who lack LDL receptors, may not have adequate uptake. To address this, investigators have conjugated a carbohydrate moiety, N-acetylgalactosamine (GalNAc), to the surface lipid layer. Because the liver contains a high density of asialoglycoprotein receptors, these receptors can selectively facilitate endocytosis of GalNAc coated LNPs into hepatocytes independent of LDL receptors. Although an elegant solution that has proven very successful with inclisiran, a GalNAc-conjugated siRNA against PCSK9, the efficacy of this approach with LNPs still requires further exploration to validate efficacy in relevant patient populations, namely homozygous FH.

Several features of PCSK9 biology make it an attractive candidate for in vivo gene therapy. First, PCSK9 is most abundantly expressed in liver whence it is secreted into circulation. Liver is known to avidly take up LNPs due in part to its important role in homeostatic regulation of circulating lipoproteins. Secondly, based on human genetics studies of PCSK9 germline (i.e. whole-body) null patients, there appear to be no negative effects of PCSK9 deletion [30]. Third, PCSK9 inhibitors have proven highly effective in reducing LDL-C and ASCVD risk in large placebo-controlled trials, thus further demonstrating that mid-life depletion of circulating PCSK9 is effective in reducing risk. Fourth, PCSK9 inhibitors are currently costly and require redosing, thus balancing out the upfront cost of gene therapy vs. a lifetime of pharmacologic inhibition; however, there are an increasing number of products competing in this space, which would be expected to reduce costs in coming years.

Pre-clinical studies were performed in human cultured primary hepatocytes, mice and monkeys to validate the concept and technology. Using an adenine base editor, Musunuru et al. mutated the mRNA splice-donor site between exons 1 and 2 of PCSK9, resulting in a retained intron and a non-sense, frame-shifted transcript [31]. Twenty gRNA sequences were tested in human and monkey hepatocytes to optimize disruption of splicing. Using the optimized sequence, later studies in wildtype monkeys by Lee et al. demonstrated knockdown of hepatic PCSK9 by 83% and serum LDL-C by 69% in the higher dose arm (1.5 mg/kg) and 67% and 49% respectively in the lower dose arm (0.75 mg/kg) [32]. These reductions persisted for more than one year after a single infusion. Editing occurred primarily in the liver, though there was also detectable editing in adrenal gland and spleen, especially at the higher dose, indicating that LNPs also dispersed there. The investigators reported no detectable editing in the monkeys’ sperm or in offspring of treated mice, and also no editing in the brain. Transient but significant elevation of AST and ALT were noted soon after infusion into monkeys, but these rapidly normalized and remained normal for the remaining year of the study. Bilirubin, insulin, fasting glucose and hemoglobin A1C were unchanged throughout the study.

Based on these encouraging preclinical results, Verve Therapeutics commercialized the technology under the name VERVE-101 and launched an exploratory open-label trial for human subjects (“Heart-1” trial; NCT05398029) [33]. This trial enrolled individuals with heterozygous FH (mean LDL-C 193 mg/dL) who had concomitant ASCVD and who were not actively treated with PCSK9 inhibitors. Early results of efficacy were in line with preclinical expectations with LDL-C lowering of 39–55% depending on dose in the ten individuals studied. As expected, there were also transient increases in liver function tests, and one participant developed asymptomatic grade 3 transaminitis and thrombocytopenia. One participant developed cardiac arrest 5 weeks after infusion not deemed to be study related and another developed a myocardial infarction considered potentially treatment related. This patient was hospitalized for observation and recovered.

In discussion with regulators, Verve halted recruitment for the VERVE-101 trial and pivoted all efforts into a trial for VERVE-102, which includes a GalNAc-conjugated lipid that is expected to facilitate LDLR-independent uptake as well as new ionizable and PEGylated lipids, both of which are intended reduce the inflammatory response [34]. Addition of the carbohydrate moiety to the LNP surface facilitates liver uptake in the setting of reduced or absent LDL receptors by targeting the asialoglycoprotein receptor, which can also mediate endocytosis and is abundantly expressed in liver [35]. Hypothetically this may result in faster clearance of LNPs from circulation after infusion, which could reduce off target dispersion to tissues such as adrenal gland, spleen and possibly atherosclerotic plaques, especially in patients with FH who have reduced or absent LDL receptors. Currently there are no published data demonstrating clearance kinetics or editing distribution in germline LDLR homozygous primates or humans.

Currently, Verve Therapeutics (USA, recently acquired by Eli Lilly) has an ongoing phase 1b trial for VERVE-102 (“Heart-2” or VT-10201 trial; NCT06164730) featuring GalNAc-coated LNPs bearing sgRNAs targeting PCSK9 and an Cas9-ABE mRNA with a commonly-used ABE derived from Escherichia coli. The gene editing machinery is unchanged from VERVE-101. In addition to the novel LNP formulation being tested, the VERVE-102 trial also includes individuals who have either heterozygous FH or premature CAD, expanding the potential scope of this therapy. Peer-reviewed interim findings were recently published for the first 35 participants, who received a single dose of 0.3, 0.45, 0.6, 0.7, 0.8, or 1.0 mg of total RNA per kg of total body weight [36]. Safety was the primary clinical outcome. Mean age of participants was 52 years. Other notable baseline characteristics include: white race 86%, male 69%, mean BMI 27, mean LDL 129, heterozygous FH 83%, high intensity statin use 71%. Safety data were consistent with prior expectations, with infusion reactions (grade 1 or 2) occurring in 20% of patients, none of which required termination of the infusion. Transient elevations in liver transaminases were also observed as expected from prior studies. One participant had an aspiration pneumonia which was deemed as unrelated to treatment. Efficacy results were notable for a dose-dependent reduction in circulating PCSK9 level that appeared to be durable in most dose groups over a maximum follow-up of 545 days. Although the highest dose arm (1.0 mg/kg) shows the greatest initial reduction in PCSK9 and LDL-C, this group only includes data up to 90 days due to recent dosing. Mean LDL-C at 28 days ranged from 114 mg/dl in the lowest dose arm to 51 mg/dl in the highest.

YolTech Therapeutics (China) also has an ongoing study of a PCSK9 gene editor, YOLT-101 (NCT06458010), using similar GalNAc-coated LNPs, but the base editor is a novel sequence that originates from Hafnia paralvei [37, 38]. Notably, the YOLT-101 study is solely enrolling patients with familial hypercholesterolemia. Peer-reviewed interim data for six study participants from this trial were recently published as well [39]. In this small cohort, no serious adverse events were noted, though there were non-severe transfusion reactions and liver enzyme elevations as expected. The highest dose single-infusion (0.6 mg/kg) was given to 3 participants and reduced circulating PCSK9 and LDL-C by 74% and 52%, respectively, similar in magnitude to preclinical expectations.

Reduction of serum PCSK9 levels by gene editing appears to be technically feasible in humans based on currently available data. Benefits are well established from published studies of PCSK9 monoclonal antibodies in reducing ASCVD risk, and gene editing appears to have a comparable effect on LDL-C; therefore, gene editing is expected to reduce lifetime ASCVD risk. Although expression of the CRISPR-Cas9 machinery is transient due to limited half-lives of mRNA and protein, effects of genomic editing will last for the remaining lifetime of the patient. This permanence applies to both on-target and off-target editing. Adenine base editing has demonstrated an impressive on-target efficiency in preclinical and clinical trials, however, it is inherently a mutagenic tool that cannot be perfectly controlled. Sporadic off-target editing, Cas9-dependent and -independent, have not been thoroughly evaluated in large animal models. This is primarily due to technical limitations in detecting rare, unique mutations in large populations of cells, even with high-throughput sequencing techniques.

The human liver contains hundreds of millions of cells which will be edited with extraordinary on-target efficiency by LNP treatment. However, when we consider even low level off-target, heterogenous mutation rates, it seems plausible that some cells will get a first or second hit towards oncogenic transformation. In an otherwise healthy young patient who undergoes gene editing, but later in life develops other risk factors for hepatocellular carcinoma such as fatty liver, alcoholism or viral hepatitis which induce chronic liver injury and clonal regeneration, there could be a large population of cells with random somatic variation exposed to selective pressures promoting cancer. Accordingly, liver oncogenic risk could take years or decades to fully manifest. Therefore, the long-term benefit/risk ratio is unknown for this novel class of drug, and further research is needed before considering extension to groups not at short term, high ASCVD risk. Of note, epigenetic editing of human PCSK9 has been reported in mouse models and non-human primates (NHP), with the potential advantages of durable effects without underlying DNA sequence changes, and potential reversibility of the gene silencing. However, human studies with this technology have not been reported to date.

Acute risks are more straightforward to assess, and current data suggest a few including infusion reactions, acute liver injury or transaminitis, thrombocytopenia and atherosclerotic plaque instability. Thus far, infusion reaction has been mild and easily managed with anti-pyretic. Acute liver injury, diagnosed by severe transaminitis, has occurred in some patients and NHPs, though it appears to follow a self-limited course. There are conceptually a variety of reasons this could occur, including lipotoxicity from the LNPs, transient off-target editing of hepatocyte RNA by the ABE, genome editing toxicity or inflammation due to expression of the gene editing machinery, which are foreign proteins derived from bacteria. Thrombocytopenia was observed in the Heart-1 trial using VERVE-101, but it is unclear if this issue persists with VERVE-102 given the small number of patients so far. One patient treated with VERVE-101 suffered a myocardial infarction soon after infusion, which was possibly related to the treatment. The FH population is at high risk of MI and plaque rupture at baseline, so this could be coincidental and unrelated; however, it is also possible that the peri-infusion inflammatory response or the LNP itself could lead to atherosclerotic plaque instability [40]. Further study is needed to differentiate between these possibilities.

Based on non-peer-reviewed preliminary results, Verve has stated that editing efficiency appears to correlate more with total RNA dose than weight-based dosing, though they do not hypothesize a mechanism for this phenomenon [41]. One possibility is dispersion of LNPs to non-target tissues, resulting in either uptake, sequestration or lysis prior to reaching the liver. These alternative pharmacologic sinks may correlate poorly with total body weight. Thus a higher total dose would ensure saturation of these sites and allow higher on-target editing in the liver in all individuals, irrespective of body composition. This hypothesis could be tested using radiolabeled LNPs in the relevant patient populations or a NHP model of familial hypercholesterolemia. Further pretreatment saturation with inert LNP could also be evaluated as a solution in a model system. Verve reports ongoing studies in NHP using CRISPR-Cas9 to generate in situ knockout of LDLR, but results are not yet published. Overall, there is still much that is unknown about LNP pharmacokinetics, especially in the FH population, and further studies will be needed to calibrate dosing and reduce off-target risks.

There are several putative therapeutic advantages to PCSK9 gene editing, most notably durability, treatment burden and efficacy (Table 2). Conceptually, these advantages are most attractive for primary prevention in younger patients at high lifetime ASCVD risk including those with multiple other traditional ASCVD risk factors, strong family history of CVD, persistent moderate dyslipidemia, and those with heterozygous FH without extreme LDL-C levels. In these individuals, there is the potential for a one-time PCSK9 gene editing therapy to replace several decades of daily or periodic medical therapy. However, this scenario requires advancements such that risks of PCSK9 gene editing must be proven to be very low, including long term harm, since these individuals are at low short term ASCVD risk. Initially anti-PCSK9 LNPs are also expected to be small scale and very expensive. Although prices for current PCSK9 editors have not yet been announced, projections from current commercial stage gene therapies suggests a potential range from tens-of-thousands to millions of dollars [42].

PCSK9 gene editing compared with currently available PCSK9-targeting therapies

For older patients treated for secondary prevention, the main advantage would be improved therapeutic adherence, with a treatment burden more similar to surgery than medical management. Currently, less than 50% of older individuals remain adherent to lipid lowering therapy two years after a myocardial infarction, and short term risk of recurrent ASCVD events remain high [43]. In this patient population, upfront cost would remain an issue for the foreseeable future, and while there may be more risk tolerance of the gene therapy, additional evidence of acceptable risk is required since there are cheaper highly effective options available that are very well tolerated.

In patients with familial hypercholesterolemia, monotherapy with high intensity statin or PCSK9 inhibitor is often inadequate to reach optimal LDL-C levels of < 70 mg/dL [44] and additional medicine is needed [45]. Thus, PCSK9 gene editing would not eliminate the need for additional lifelong lipid-lowering therapies. In the case of homozygous FH, the treatment burden can be quite significant, including onerous LDL apheresis treatments, thus debulking the regimen would be a reasonable goal. However, PCSK9 modifying therapies are overall less effective in individuals with homozygous FH, with no LDL-C change in those with null LDL receptor mutations [46, 47]. These patients can be treated with an ANGPTL3 inhibitor whose therapeutic action is independent of LDL receptors [48]. In parallel to PCSK9 gene editing trials, ANGPTL3 is also being investigated for gene editing, with encouraging results published recently [49, 50]. In the future, these targets possibly could be multiplexed for co-editing by including both sgRNAs in the LNPs.

This is an exciting time for Preventative Cardiology with a massive recent expansion in the pharmacologic options for reduction of ASCVD risk. It is also an exciting time for gene therapy with the application of CRISPR-Cas9 technology for permanent, tissue-specific gene editing. Early peer-reviewed clinical results suggest good on-target efficacy for reducing PCSK9 and LDL-C. Viewing these gene editing vectors as customizable platforms for liver editing, it is intriguing to consider editing other lipid-lowering targets or even multiplexing of multiple targets into a single infusion. Nonetheless, potential for acute adverse events remains a concern, though it is difficult to assess the magnitude of these risks without further study in larger cohorts. Latent adverse outcomes, such as oncogenicity and cirrhosis or effects in non-target tissues, are unknown and require monitoring in longitudinal trials. Therefore, current clinical investigations should focus on patients with highest short-term ASCVD risk. Furthermore, outcomes trials will be needed to evaluate whether potential ASCVD benefits exceed risk of complications on relevant time scales.
